messages:
nora: quick sync — ran an input-aware quant prototype that switches between fp8/int8 at token boundaries based on query entropies. interesting results: gains on short-turn QA but weird hallucination spikes on chained reasoning prompts.
diego: can you paste a minimal repro? curious about the decision boundary and hysteresis.
nora: minimal repro below — take a chain-of-thought prompt, the model flips to fp8 for first 3 tokens, then int8 later; hallucination appears after the switch.
```
# pseudo
prompt = 'Q: How does X relate to Y? Think step-by-step.'
# runtime decides: token_entropy > 4.0 -> use fp8 else int8
```

marta: is this the runtime switching inside the same KV cache? or does it flush / rekey? that could explain state divergence.
linh: if we change numeric path mid-sequence and keep same cached KV layout we must ensure rounding semantics are consistent. small bias accumulates. switching without reconcilation is risky.
diego: ops concern: switching in-flight makes shard-local caches non-deterministic across replicas, hurts dedup and cross-tenant caching and makes debugging harder.
nora: prototype kept the KV format unchanged, only changed compute quant path. hypothesis: quant rounding noise on early tokens perturbs attention weights which cascades.
marta: two high-level proposals: 1) conservative approach: only switch between profiles at request boundaries (no in-flight switching) + use shadow-eval to pick profile per-request. 2) aggressive approach: allow in-flight switching but with reconciliation layer that recalibrates cached KV by rescaling cached keys/values when switching.
linh: reconcilation idea: store per-kv-block scale metadata and apply a single multiplier when changing compute path. cheap if we keep metadata as one float per block. downside: extra read/write on hot path.
diego: alternative: prefer predictive switching (decide profile before generation by scoring the prompt) — avoids mid-sequence changes entirely. you pay slightly more latency pre-decision but far less complexity.
nora: predictive model worked well in offline experiments for >90% cases. failures were in long multi-turn where later tokens need different precision.
marta: for long multi-turn we could do hybrid: predictive for initial decision, then allow mid-sequence hints only when a trusted detector fires (and we then do a full reconcile). requires detector confidence tracking.
ops-bot: warning: per-request-profile variance increases cache key cardinality. estimate: if we allow N profiles and M tenants, cache keys multiply by N*M. watch memory.
diego: to limit explosion, namespace cache by profile-trust-level only (experimental/canary/stable) instead of full profile id. good middle ground.
linh: config sketch for API surface (small, ergonomic):
```
precision_hint: {
  mode: "predictive|static|adaptive",
  preferred_profile: "fp8-safe|int8"  # optional
  trace_id: "p-1755550001"
}
```

marta: telemetry we need: pre_decision_profile, actual_profile_sequence (comma-separated), fidelity_loss, late_token_divergence. also store detector_confidence when applicable.
nora: rollout plan suggestion: beta with predictive-only mode for 5 tenants, shadow adaptive mode for another 5, gather fidelity_loss over 48h, abort if fidelity_loss > 0.03 or hallucination-rate uptick > 1.5x.
diego: tests: unit shadow evals + replay harness that replays same random seeds across profile variants and compares token-likelihood deltas + embedding drift.
linh: implementation note: reconcile multiplier should be stored as single-precision float in metadata and applied lazily on read to avoid extra writes.
marta: action items: @nora run predictive-vs-adaptive comparison and attach sample failure cases; @linh prototype lazy-reconcile metadata and benchmark p99 latency; @diego estimate cache cardinality and propose eviction caps; ops-bot: create canary job template.
ops-bot: canary template created: canary/quant-adaptive/1755550001 -> queued
marta: final ask — avoid adding new required request fields. make precision_hint optional so existing clients unaffected. we'll document trust levels and default behavior in the RFC update. :rocket:
